Hacker News #5

Ladybird is now in alpha

Ladybird is now in alpha

科技产品 作者 janvdberg 热度 2166 回复 524 2026/11/24 00:13
打开原帖 打开外部链接 JSON

摘要

  • Hello friends! Ladybird is now in alpha. You can download it for macOS and Linux. I’ve been looking forward to writing this post for a long time. :^) Ladybird is a browser with a new engine. The engine is our own, built from the ground up, and not a fork. The browser around it is modest, but functional. This is an alpha, so some websites won’t work, and it will crash sometimes. When that happens, tell us! You can report a broken site from inside the browser. After a crash, you can read the crash report and decide whether to send it. Our privacy policy has the details. We want security nerds to hack it! A new browser gets hacked, over and over, and that’s part of the process, so we make no promises about security today. When you pwn us, please tell us how so we can harden Ladybird! The alpha is a rolling channel, and we’ll be pushing out automatic updates regularly. This is the part I’m most excited about. Ladybird improves quickly, and until now you had to build it from source to see that. If you build websites, try yours in Ladybird and tell us what breaks. It supports WebDriver for automated testing, as well as the Firefox DevTools protocol. Thank you to our sponsors and donors, and to everyone who has tested, reported bugs, and written code over the years. There’s still a mountain of work ahead of us, but I’m very happy that you can finally try Ladybird for yourself!

simscitizen 2026/11/24 05:55
Browsers are runtimes and webpages are apps. They just happen to be apps that are dynamically fetched over the network and are packaged as HTML/CSS/JS instead of as PE/ELF/Mach-O binaries.

Runtimes can have bugs or inefficiencies that cause them to use more memory than strictly necessary, but by and large most memory problems are the product of the apps (or webpages) themselves.

panta 2026/11/24 15:33
The view of web pages as apps and browsers as runtime environments/OSes is reasonable but in my opinion it even reinforces the idea that it should be the browser duty to contain bad behavior from web apps/pages. Browsers are well positioned to do so, as they know exactly which resources are used by each tab , and how those grow over time. Also browsers already treat web content as untrusted (sandboxing, isolation), so it would be a natural next step to extend that approach to resource usage. It would match how Operating Systems work, where it's the OS acting as an "arbiter", not the userland application.

mkgiga 2026/11/24 14:47
It's a difficult question because there are so many factors in dom/css that change the answer to 'is there a chance that the image should be rendered the next frame?' that it becomes really hard to implement a strategy for what content to offload to disk and when

If the runtime fails to load the offloaded data back in time there will be visible rendering artifacts so you really have to make sure your strategy is robust
